etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English swētere, equivalent to sweat +‎ -er.

definitions.definition: A knitted jacket or jersey, usually of thick wool, worn by athletes before or after exercise.
(US) A similar garment worn for warmth.

quote.citation: 1997, “Autumn Sweater”, in I Can Hear the Heart Beating as One, performed by Yo La Tengo:
quote.text: We could slip away / Wouldn't that be better? / Me with nothing to say / And you in your autumn sweater

quote.citation: 2007, John T. James, A Sea of Broken Hearts: Patient Rights in a Dangerous Profit-Driven Health Care System, →ISBN, page 29:
quote.text: The cardiologist who administered Alex's exercise stress test on August 21 observed during that test that Alex was a profuse sweater.

definitions.definition: One who or that which causes to sweat.

quote.text: We learn of the cruelty of some school or child-factory from journalists; we learn it from inspectors, we learn it from doctors, we learn it even from shame-stricken schoolmasters and repentant sweaters; but we never learn it from the children; we never learn it from the victims.

definitions.definition: (historical) An exploitative middleman who subcontracted piece work in the tailoring trade.

quote.citation: 1894, New York (State) Bureau of Mediation and Arbitration, Annual Report (volumes 7-8, page 158)
quote.text: If the piecework system had not existed there never would have been any sweatees. The men who are sweaters, I am sorry to say, are men who formerly belonged to our union.

definitions.definition: (archaic) One who sweats coins, i.e. removes small portions by shaking them.
(UK, obsolete) A London street ruffian in Queen Anne's time who prodded passers-by with his sword-point.

quote.citation: William Lecky, quoted in 1965, Gilbert Geis, Juvenile Gangs (page 6)
quote.text: Among them were the "sweaters" who formed a circle round their prisoner and pricked him with their swords until he sank exhausted to the ground,  […]
